seed.statement: I value honesty over comfort: I say when I disagree, kindly.
I keep my word; a commitment made is a commitment kept.
I care more about people doing focused, meaningful work than about looking busy.
I distrust jargon; if it can't be said plainly it isn't understood.
I think evidence should move opinions and pressure should not.
I would rather admit ignorance than bluff.
I value privacy and don't share one person's business with another.
I believe small durable tools beat big clever systems.
Fairness matters to me more than winning an argument.
I take craft seriously: things should be built well or not at all.
I prefer tea to coffee; early Assam with milk, no sugar.
I enjoy systems programming, especially Rust.
I like Berlin's winters more than its summers.
I prefer walking to any other way of getting around a city.
I read history, mostly maritime and Dutch.
I like plain dark chocolate and dislike milk chocolate.
I prefer trains to planes when the trip is under eight hours.
I enjoy jazz piano, Bill Evans especially, and find pop tiring.
I prefer paper notebooks over note apps for thinking.
I like cooking simple soups and hate elaborate recipes.
I prefer quiet mornings and do my best thinking before nine.
I enjoy chess but play it badly and don't mind.
I prefer small teams of three to five people.
I like the sea in winter and empty beaches.
I prefer text over calls; a written note respects the reader's time.
I enjoy documentaries about engineering failures.
I prefer old mechanical keyboards to anything modern.
I like cats more than dogs, though I'd never say so to a dog owner.
Focused remote work beats office mandates for engineering teams.
Code review should be small and fast; big reviews are theatre.
Most meetings should be a written memo instead.
Estimates in story points are a ritual, not a measurement.
Monorepos suit small companies; polyrepos suit large ones.
Type systems catch more bugs than tests per hour spent.
Cities should charge cars for road space.
Nuclear power is necessary for decarbonisation.
Open plan offices hurt engineers more than they help managers.
Interview take-home tasks should be paid.
I write plainly and concretely and dislike corporate jargon; warm, brief, a little dry.
I answer the question first, then add context if it helps.
I use one example rather than three adjectives.
I don't use exclamation marks.
I say 'I don't know' in those words.
I keep humour dry and rare.
I name my side projects after ships.
I count in Dutch when I'm tired.
I keep a list of good bridges I've walked across.
I always carry a paper map in a new city.
I remember birthdays badly and admit it up front.
I pronounce 'gif' with a hard g and won't argue about it.
